meta.topic: UI, API and database values differ

problem:
Meridian Bank has a cross-border payment complaint that looks simple and turns out not to be: the customer sees one amount in the online banking screen, the API transmitted a different amount, and the persisted record in the database holds a third value. The payment also carries a beneficiary address that appears complete in the user interface but arrives truncated in the payment message. The customer wants to know which value is correct, and the bank cannot answer until it traces one record through every layer it passed through. Each team defends its own layer: the channel team says the screen shows what the customer entered, the API team says the payload was valid, and the database team says the record is what was stored.

The learner must trace the record layer by layer using a stable identifier, and find the first point where the value changes incorrectly. The causes to consider are concrete: a transformation that rounds or converts, a timezone shift on a date, a mapping that drops a field, a stale cache serving an old read model, an asynchronous update that has not yet landed, or a field truncation in the message mapping. The address issue adds a scheme rule: a structured or hybrid address is required, with a minimum of Town Name and Country Code, or BIC only, and the bank must not teach a fixed structured-address cut-off date, since the deadline was extended in July 2026 and a new timeline is expected by December 2026. The case also tests the MT to MX boundary: where a legacy message lacks a value the ISO 20022 message needs, the bank must never fabricate it.
solution:
Start by fixing the record: pick one affected payment and its stable identifier, such as the end-to-end identification, and use that single identifier at every layer so the comparison is about the same record. Capture the value at each point: what the customer entered and what the screen displayed, the API request payload as received, the transformed canonical model, the validation and defaulting applied, the database write, and the read model or cache that serves the screen. Compare the values in order and mark the first layer where the value changes without a documented rule. Check the usual suspects at that layer: decimal precision and rounding, currency conversion, timezone conversion on dates, character encoding, field truncation, a mapping that drops or merges fields, a stale cache, and an asynchronous update that has not yet been applied.

For the address, check the mapping from the channel fields to the message: whether the structured or hybrid address carries Town Name and Country Code as a minimum, whether any field is truncated by a length limit, and whether the mapping preserves the address the customer entered. Where a legacy MT message lacks a value the ISO 20022 message requires, do not fabricate it: check whether the value can be derived from trusted contextual data such as the settlement arrangement, document the derivation rule, and hold the payment for repair if no reliable derivation exists. Once the divergence is found, assign the fix to the owning layer, correct the affected record through a controlled process, and add a lineage check so the same field is compared across layers in regression testing.

decision.question: Meridian Bank receives a cross-border payment complaint: the customer sees one amount on screen, the API transmitted another, and the database holds a third. The beneficiary address also arrives truncated in the payment message. You are the business analyst asked to trace the record and find the first point of divergence.

options.label: A
options.detail: Trust the database value, since the database is the system of record and the other layers must be wrong.

options.label: B
options.detail: Fix the screen to show the database value, since the customer only sees the screen.

options.label: C
options.detail: Ask the customer to resubmit the payment with the correct amount, since the original is already confused.

options.label: D
options.detail: Trace one affected record by its stable identifier through UI, API payload, transformation, persistence and read model, comparing values at each layer to find the first divergence.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because only a layer-by-layer trace with a stable identifier can show where a value first changes incorrectly. Option A assumes the answer without evidence. Option C creates a second payment on top of an unresolved one. Option B hides the divergence instead of fixing it.

steps.title: Select one affected record and its stable identifier for the trace
Provide the screen value and the customer input as captured
Provide the API request payload as received
Show the canonical transformation, validation and defaulting applied
Provide the persisted record and the write timestamp
Compare values layer by layer and mark the first divergence
Fix the layer, correct the record and add a lineage check

happy: The first point of divergence is evidenced and assigned to the owning layer, the affected record is corrected through a controlled process, and the address mapping carries the required structured or hybrid address without truncation. The lineage check runs in regression testing so the same field is compared across layers before the next release.

negative.title: Rounding changes the amount
negative.detail: A transformation rounds the amount to two decimals at the wrong step. Correct the precision rule, document it in the field dictionary, and revalidate affected records.

negative.title: Stale cache serves an old value
negative.detail: The screen reads a cached read model that has not yet received the latest update. Invalidate or refresh the cache on write, and show the authoritative value while the update is pending.

negative.title: Address field truncated in mapping
negative.detail: The message mapping cuts the address to a length the scheme does not support. Fix the mapping to carry the full structured or hybrid address with Town Name and Country Code as a minimum.

negative.title: Mandatory MX value absent in MT source
negative.detail: A legacy MT message lacks a value the ISO 20022 message requires. Do not fabricate the value; derive it only from trusted contextual data with a documented rule, or hold the payment for repair.

technical: Create a field lineage record for the affected fields: source system, field name, transformation rule, owner, and the layer where each change happens. Store the captured values at each layer with the record identifier, timestamp and source log, using masked production evidence where customer data is involved. Keep the source-to-target mapping with its version, the derivation catalogue for any derived value, and the original source message for audit. Log every correction with operator, old and new value, timestamp and checker.

accounting: Until the divergence is resolved, the payment must not be released on an uncertain amount or address: hold it in a controlled state and reconcile the screen value, the API payload and the database record against the ledger entry before release. If the persisted amount differs from the amount the customer authorised, the customer must be told and must confirm the corrected instruction. Operations need a data-quality worklist for records whose layers disagree, with ageing and service levels, and a rule that no operator corrects a financial amount without a second approval and a full audit record.

questions.question: What is the first step in tracing a value that differs across layers?
options: Pick one record and follow its stable identifier through every layer
questions.explanation: A single stable identifier, such as the end-to-end identification, keeps the comparison about the same record at every layer.

questions.question: What must never be done when a legacy MT message lacks a value the ISO 20022 message needs?
options: Fabricate a value to fill the field
Derive it from trusted data with a documented rule
questions.explanation: A value must never be fabricated; it is derived only from trusted contextual data with a documented rule, or the payment is held for repair.

questions.question: Which fields are the minimum for a structured or hybrid address?
options: Town Name and Country Code, or BIC only
questions.explanation: The requirement stands at structured or hybrid address with a minimum of Town Name and Country Code, or BIC only.

questions.question: Why is a fixed structured-address cut-off date not taught in this case?
options: The deadline was extended in July 2026 and a new timeline is expected by December 2026
It only applies to domestic payments
It applies only to direct debits
questions.explanation: The SWIFT structured-address deadline was extended in July 2026, so no fixed cut-off date should be taught.
